claim: Use an SCP to limit the permissions of IAM principals inside the organization's member accounts; use an RCP to restrict principals outside the organization that request access to resources in member accounts.
question: When do you choose an SCP and when an RCP?

values.display: Use an SCP when you need to limit permissions
Use an RCP when you need to restrict IAM principals

evidence.quote: Use an SCP when you need to limit permissions of IAM principals within your organization's member accounts.
Use an RCP when you need to restrict IAM principals that are external to your organization accounts making requests to access resources within your organization’s member accounts.

claim: RCPs are available only in an organization that has all features enabled, not with consolidated billing only.
question: Can an organization with only consolidated billing use RCPs?

values.display: available only in an organization that has all features enabled
RCPs aren't available

evidence.quote: RCPs are available only in an organization that has all features enabled. RCPs aren't available if your organization has enabled only the consolidated billing features.

claim: An RCP affects only resources owned by accounts in the organization that attached it: it applies to a bucket in a member account even when users from an outside account access it, but not to resources in that outside account.
question: Does an RCP apply to resources in accounts outside the organization?

values.display: affect only resources
They don't affect resources from accounts outside the organization

evidence.quote: RCPs affect only resources that are managed by accounts that are part of the organization which has attached the RCPs. They don't affect resources from accounts outside the organization.
That RCP applies to the S3 bucket in Account A even when accessed by users from Account B. However, that RCP does not apply to resources in Account B when accessed by users in Account A.

claim: If an RCP blocks a permission at any level above an account, a resource in that account does not have the permission, even when its owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows full access.
question: Can a resource-based policy that allows full access override an RCP?

values.display: a resource in the affected account does not have that permission
allows full access to any user

qualifiers.scope: resources in member accounts with an applicable RCP

evidence.quote: If a permission is blocked at any level above the account, a resource in the affected account does not have that permission, even if the resource owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows full access to any user.

claim: RCPs do not apply to AWS managed keys in AWS KMS.
question: Do RCPs apply to AWS managed KMS keys?

values.display: RCPs do not apply to AWS managed keys
You cannot change or manage their permissions

qualifiers.scope: AWS managed keys for AWS KMS

evidence.quote: RCPs do not apply to AWS managed keys for AWS Key Management Service. AWS managed keys are created, managed, and used on your behalf by an AWS service. You cannot change or manage their permissions.

claim: When RCPs are enabled, the AWS managed policy RCPFullAWSAccess is attached to the root, every OU and every account; it cannot be detached, it lets all requests pass RCP evaluation, and it does not grant access.
question: What is the RCPFullAWSAccess policy, and can it be detached?

values.display: RCPFullAWSAccess
You cannot detach this policy
This AWS managed policy does not grant access

qualifiers.scope: organization root, every OU and every account

evidence.quote: It is automatically attached to the organization root, every OU, and every account in your organization, when you enable resource control policies (RCPs). You cannot detach this policy. This default RCP allows all principals and actions access to pass through RCP evaluation, meaning until you start creating and attaching RCPs, all your existing IAM permissions continue to operate as they did. This AWS managed policy does not grant access.

claim: In RCPs the Allow effect is supported only for the RCPFullAWSAccess policy, so custom RCPs use Deny statements.
question: Can a custom RCP use an Allow statement?

values.display: The effect of Allow is only supported
You can make use of Deny statements

evidence.quote: The effect of Allow is only supported for the RCPFullAWSAccess policy.
You can make use of Deny statements to block access to resources in your organization.

claim: A declarative policy centrally declares and enforces the desired configuration of an AWS service across the organization, and the configuration stays enforced when the service adds new features or APIs.
question: What does a declarative policy do, and what happens when the service adds new APIs?

values.display: centrally declare and enforce your desired configuration
the configuration is always maintained

evidence.quote: Declarative policies allow you to centrally declare and enforce your desired configuration for a given AWS service at scale across an organization. Once attached, the configuration is always maintained when the service adds new features or APIs.

claim: Declarative policies prevent noncompliant actions; for example, they can block public internet access to Amazon VPC resources or enforce encryption in transit for VPC traffic across the organization.
question: Give an example of what a declarative policy can enforce.

values.display: Use declarative policies to prevent noncompliant actions
block public internet access to Amazon VPC resources

evidence.quote: Use declarative policies to prevent noncompliant actions. For example, you can block public internet access to Amazon VPC resources, or enforce encryption in transit for VPC traffic, across your organization.

claim: Declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane: authorization policies regulate access to APIs, while declarative policies are applied directly at the service level.
question: How does a declarative policy differ from an SCP or RCP in where it is enforced?

values.display: enforced in the service's control plane
authorization policies regulate access to APIs

qualifiers.scope: declarative policies compared with SCPs and RCPs

evidence.quote: Declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane, which is an important distinction from authorization policies such as service control policies (SCPs) and resource control policies (RCPs).
While authorization policies regulate access to APIs, declarative policies are applied directly at the service level to enforce durable intent.

claim: Declarative policies govern service-linked roles; SCPs and RCPs do not.
question: Which organization policy type governs service-linked roles?

values.display: Governs service-linked roles?
No | No | Yes

evidence.quote: | Governs service-linked roles? | No | No | Yes |
evidence.table_header: |  | Service control policies | Resource control policies | Declarative policies |

claim: Accounts that join an organization inherit its declarative policies automatically, and when a declarative policy is detached the attribute rolls back to its state before the policy was attached.
question: What happens with declarative policies when an account joins, and when the policy is detached?

values.display: will automatically inherit the declarative policy
the attribute state will roll back

evidence.quote: Accounts joining an organization will automatically inherit the declarative policy in the organization.
If a declarative policy is detached, the attribute state will roll back to its previous state before the declarative policy was attached.

claim: A declarative policy attached to the root is inherited by all OUs and accounts; attached to an OU it is inherited by accounts directly under it or under any child OU; attached to an account it affects only that account.
question: How are declarative (management) policies inherited down the organization tree?

values.display: all OUs and accounts in the organization inherit that policy
it affects only that account

qualifiers.scope: declarative policy inheritance (not SCPs or RCPs)

evidence.quote: When you attach a declarative policy to the organization root, all OUs and accounts in the organization inherit that policy.
When you attach a declarative policy to a specific OU, accounts that are directly under that OU or any child OU inherit the policy.
When you attach a declarative policy to a specific account, it affects only that account.

claim: The effective declarative policy of an account is the set of rules inherited from the root and OUs plus those attached directly to the account; it is the final set of rules that apply.
question: What is the effective policy of an account?

values.display: the set of rules that are inherited
specifies the final set of rules

evidence.quote: The effective policy is the set of rules that are inherited from the organization root and OUs along with those directly attached to the account. The effective policy specifies the final set of rules that apply to the account.

claim: Tag policies standardize tags on resources in the organization's accounts; untagged resources and tags not defined in the tag policy are not evaluated for compliance.
question: What do tag policies do, and do they act on untagged resources?

values.display: standardize the tags attached to the AWS resources
Untagged resources or tags that aren't defined
aren't evaluated for compliance with the tag policy

evidence.quote: Tag policies allow you to standardize the tags attached to the AWS resources in your organization's accounts.
Untagged resources or tags that aren't defined in the tag policy aren't evaluated for compliance with the tag policy.

claim: A tag policy can enforce compliance on specified resource types, which prevents noncompliant tagging requests on those resource types from completing.
question: Can a tag policy block a noncompliant tagging request?

values.display: noncompliant tagging operations on specified resource types are enforced
are prevented from completing

qualifiers.condition: enforcement set for the resource type

evidence.quote: A tag policy can also specify that noncompliant tagging operations on specified resource types are enforced. In other words, noncompliant tagging requests on specified resource types are prevented from completing.

claim: Backup policies centrally apply AWS Backup plans to resources across the organization's accounts; the effective backup plan appears in each account as an immutable plan that can be viewed but not changed.
question: What do backup policies do, and can a member account change the resulting backup plan?

values.display: centrally manage and apply backup plans
as an immutable plan for that account
You can view it, but not change it

evidence.quote: Backup policies allow you to centrally manage and apply backup plans to the AWS resources across an organization's accounts.
The effective backup plan for each AWS account in the organization appears in the AWS Backup console as an immutable plan for that account. You can view it, but not change it.

claim: An AI services opt-out policy lets the organization opt out of AWS AI services using and storing its content for service improvement; opting out deletes the associated historical content shared before.
question: What do AI services opt-out policies do?

values.display: opt out of use of your content for service improvement
deletes all of the associated historical content

evidence.quote: You can opt out of use of your content for service improvement by using the AWS Organizations opt-out policy.
When you opt out of content use by an AWS AI service, that service deletes all of the associated historical content that was shared with AWS before you set the option.

claim: SCPs are meant as coarse-grained guardrails that do not grant access, and the AWS example SCPs use a deny-list strategy that also needs FullAWSAccess or another allowing policy attached.
question: How are the AWS example SCPs meant to be used?

values.display: coarse-grained guardrails
use a deny list strategy

evidence.quote: Service control policies (SCPs) are meant to be used as coarse-grained guardrails, and they don't directly grant access.

The SCP examples in this repository use a deny list strategy, which means that you also need a FullAWSAccess policy or other policy that allows access attached to your organization entities to allow actions.
